claim: The MAPK family of proteins is a ubiquitous signaling element in eukaryotes.
source: The MAPK family of proteins is a ubiquitous signaling element in eukaryotes, and is essential to the function of a wide variety of cellular behaviors, from the regulation of differentiation and proliferation to stress responses and more (Cargnello and Roux, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cargnello and Roux, 2011

claim: The MAPK family is essential to the function of a wide variety of cellular behaviors, from the regulation of differentiation and proliferation to stress responses.
source: The MAPK family of proteins is a ubiquitous signaling element in eukaryotes, and is essential to the function of a wide variety of cellular behaviors, from the regulation of differentiation and proliferation to stress responses and more (Cargnello and Roux, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cargnello and Roux, 2011

claim: The diversity of MAPK functions has been made possible by the evolutionary expansion of the MAPK repertoire.
source: this diversity of functions has been made possible by the evolutionary expansion of the MAPK repertoire (Caffrey et al., 1999; Manning et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Caffrey et al., 1999 and Manning et al., 2002

claim: The amino acids in the immediate vicinity of the phosphorylated residue help to dictate whether the substrate is phosphorylated by the kinase.
source: Following the association of the kinase and substrate, the amino acids in the immediate vicinity of the phosphorylated residue – together making up the 'phospho-motif' – help to dictate whether the substrate is phosphorylated by the kinase (Mok et al., 2010; Howard et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mok et al., 2010 and Howard et al., 2014

claim: It is the site that is phosphorylated – rather than the kinase itself – that mediates the functional outcome of kinase regulation.
source: However, it is the site that is phosphorylated – rather than the kinase itself – that mediates the functional outcome of kinase regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinase regulation based on established knowledge

claim: The phosphorylated phospho-motif can be recognized by a regulatory protein bearing a phospho-motif binding domain and control protein localization or degradation.
source: In particular, the phosphorylated phospho-motif can be recognized by a regulatory protein bearing a phospho-motif binding domain and control protein localization or degradation among many other effects (Seet et al., 2006; Bhattacharyya et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Seet et al., 2006 and Bhattacharyya et al., 2006

claim: The kinase and substrate must be colocalized before the kinase can interact with the phospho-motif.
source: Even before the kinase has a chance to interact with the phospho-motif, the two proteins must be colocalized (Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ubersax and Ferrell, 2007

claim: Residues apart from the kinase active site are frequently responsible for recognizing a substrate.
source: Residues apart from the kinase active site are frequently responsible for recognizing a substrate
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The transcription factor Tec1 has been shown to be both a substrate for Fus3 and Cdc4.
source: The transcription factor Tec1 fulfills these criteria, as it has been shown to be both a substrate for Fus3 and Cdc4 (Chou et al., 2004; Bao et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou et al., 2004 and Bao et al., 2010

claim: Fus3 targeted to YFP via PDZ ligand-mPDZ interaction with a functional Tec1 phosphodegron results in a ~3.7-fold drop in YFP fluorescence upon α-factor induction.
source: We observed a ~3.7-fold drop in the yeast strain containing both the Fus3-mPDZ ligand fusion and our new YFP-degron-mPDZ construct (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The drop in YFP fluorescence was not observed when the phospho-acceptor residues in the degron were changed to methionine and alanine.
source: On the other hand, the drop in fluorescence was not observed when the phospho-acceptor residues in the degron (two threonine residues) were changed to methionine and alanine (Bao et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citation to Bao et al., 2010 for the mutation strategy

claim: The drop in YFP fluorescence was not observed when the catalytic site of the targeted kinase was inactivated with a K42R mutation.
source: the drop in fluorescence was not observed when...the catalytic site of the targeted kinase was inactivated with a K42R mutation (Gartner et al., 1992)
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citation to Gartner et al., 1992 for the mutation

claim: The drop in YFP fluorescence was not observed when the interaction domain fused to YFP was changed to an SH3 domain.
source: the drop in fluorescence was not observed when...the interaction domain fused to YFP was changed to an SH3 domain
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The Tec1 degron is not able to directly recruit Fus3 to the YFP construct on its own.
source: The latter suggests that the Tec1 degron is not able to directly recruit Fus3 to the YFP construct on its own.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mismatched interaction domains do not result in degradation

claim: The drop in YFP fusion protein level was sensitive to the presence of the proteasomal inhibitor MG132.
source: Finally, we also found that the drop in YFP fusion protein level was sensitive to the presence of the proteasomal inhibitor MG132, strongly suggesting that the construct was indeed being tagged and actively degraded (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Endogenous Fus3 can be re-targeted by inserting the sequence encoding the PDZ ligand downstream of the native FUS3 gene.
source: We found that by inserting the sequence encoding the PDZ ligand downstream of the native copy of the FUS3 gene in the yeast genome, the native kinase could just as efficiently cause the degradation of the YFP substrate (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: An interaction domain and a phospho-motif are necessary and sufficient to target the regulation of a native signal transduction cascade to a substrate of choice.
source: These results – along with those discussed above – imply that an interaction domain and a phospho-motif are necessary and sufficient to target the regulation of a native signal transduction cascade to a substrate of choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented

claim: Fus3 targeted to YFP via SH3 domain-SH3 ligand interaction results in ~10.1-fold degradation of the reporter.
source: We built variants of our Fus3-substrate pair with the naturally occurring SH3 domain or the synthetic SYNZIP domain (Figure 2A) (Dueber et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2012). In both cases we observed significant reporter degradation, ~10.1-fold in the case of SH3
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Dueber et al., 2009 and Thompson et al., 2012

claim: Fus3 targeted to YFP via SYNZIP domain interaction results in ~4.7-fold degradation of the reporter.
source: In both cases we observed significant reporter degradation, ~10.1-fold in the case of SH3 and ~4.7-fold for SYNZIP domains versus a control with a degron in which the two threonine residues in the Cdc4 binding site had been switched to a methionine or alanine (Figures 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The association of the protein domains PYL and ABI can be controlled using the small-molecule plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA).
source: The association of the protein domains PYL and ABI can be controlled using the small-molecule plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) (Figure 2A, right side) (Liang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 2A

claim: A change in YFP fluorescent signal was observed only when the concentration of ABA was 1 μM or higher in the ABI-PYL system.
source: When we fused these domains to Fus3 and our YFP-phosphodegron reporter, we observed a change in the fluorescent signal only when the concentration of ABA was 1 μM or higher (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The identity of the interaction domain fused to the YFP-phosphodegron target influenced the steady-state fluorescence of the reporter.
source: However, it is important to note that the identity of the interaction domain fused to the YFP-phosphodegron target influenced the steady-state fluorescence of the reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In the presence of α-factor alone, only the mCherry signal was reduced while the YFP value remained unchanged in the dual-targeting system.
source: In the presence of α-factor alone only the mCherry signal was reduced, while the YFP value remained unchanged.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation in the dual-targeting experiment

claim: When both α-factor and ABA were added, a drop in the YFP signal was observed in the dual-targeting system.
source: Only when both α-factor and ABA were added, did we see a drop in the YFP signal (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: The net fold change of the ABA-sensitive YFP-phosphodegron reporter was moderately reduced when there were two parallel MAPK-substrate systems in the same cell compared to when it was present on its own.
source: However, we noticed that when there were two parallel MAPK-substrate systems in the same cell the net fold change of the ABA-sensitive YFP-phosphodegron reporter was moderately reduced compared to when it was present on its own—from ~2.15 to ~1.85 fold.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation comparing single and dual systems

claim: A diminished response in YFP degradation was observed in the presence of a competing copy of Fus3.
source: To examine this question we constructed strains that expressed our standard system – one kinase targeting one substrate – and added either a competing copy of Fus3 or a competing substrate. In both experiments we observed a diminished response in YFP degradation in the presence of the competitor (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: A diminished response in YFP degradation was observed in the presence of a competing substrate.
source: To examine this question we constructed strains that expressed our standard system – one kinase targeting one substrate – and added either a competing copy of Fus3 or a competing substrate. In both experiments we observed a diminished response in YFP degradation in the presence of the competitor (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: As the number of phosphodegrons increased from one to three, a concurrent increase in the rate of degradation of the reporter was observed.
source: As we increased the number of phosphodegrons from one to three, we observed a concurrent increase in the rate of degradation of the reporter
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: Adding more than three phosphodegrons to the reporter did not seem to affect the rate of degradation further.
source: adding more than three phosphodegrons to the reporter did not seem to affect the rate of degradation further (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Increasing the number of phosphodegrons decreased the steady state expression of the reporter.
source: In addition to changing the degradation dynamics, increasing the number of phosphodegrons also decreased the steady state expression of the reporter, possibly by multiplying the weaker interactions of the un-phosphorylated degron(s) with the degradation machinery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Two phosphodegron variants that more closely mimicked the Cdc4 consensus motif had a decreased rate of degradation relative to the phosphodegron derived from Tec1.
source: We constructed two additional variants of the phosphodegron motif that more closely mimicked the amino acid sequence of the published 'consensus motif' for the WD40 domain of Cdc4 (Figure 3A) (Nash et al., 2001; Orlicky et al., 2003). The sequences of the two variants only differ at one site — two residues N-terminal of the phosphorylated threonine — where the Cdc4 consensus leucine was changed to a proline, an amino acid that is supposed to be preferred by Fus3 (Mok et al., 2010). Both variants had similar behaviors, with a similarly decreased rate of degradation relative to the phosphodegron derived from Tec1. (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Nash et al., 2001, Orlicky et al., 2003, and Mok et al., 2010

claim: Native ERK2 has been shown to regulate protein stability via phosphodegrons.
source: Native ERK2 has been shown to regulate protein stability via phosphodegrons
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: A phosphodegron found in the protein MKP1 is targeted by ERK2 and subsequently tagged by the ubiquitin machinery and degraded.
source: for example, a phosphodegron found in the protein MKP1 is targeted by ERK2 and subsequently tagged by the ubiquitin machinery and degraded (Lin and Yang, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin and Yang, 2006

claim: In strains with active ERK2 targeting the functional YFP reporter, fluorescence did not rise above background levels.
source: In strains with the active kinase targeting the functional YFP reporter, fluorescence did not rise above background levels (Figure 5B)—suggesting that the substrate is actively targeted, phosphorylated and then degraded.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Fluorescence was significantly higher in control strains where the interaction domain, the phosphodegron or both were missing or inactivated.
source: Fluorescence was significantly higher in control strains where the interaction domain, the phosphodegron or both were missing or inactivated (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The interaction domains and the phosphodegron are necessary and sufficient for retargeting the regulation of ERK2.
source: These results indicate that the interaction domains and the phosphodegron are necessary and sufficient for retargeting the regulation of ERK2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with ERK2

claim: The rewiring approach is potentially applicable to a wide range of MAPKs.
source: Importantly, these results also strongly suggest that this rewiring approach is potentially applicable to a wide range of MAPKs.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful retargeting of both Fus3 and ERK2

claim: Negative feedback through Ste5 reduced the maximal pathway activation by ~60% relative to untargeted controls.
source: Relative to the untargeted controls, the negative feedback through Ste5 or Ste7 reduced the maximal pathway activation in those backgrounds by ~60% and ~45%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: Negative feedback through Ste7 reduced the maximal pathway activation by ~45% relative to untargeted controls.
source: Relative to the untargeted controls, the negative feedback through Ste5 or Ste7 reduced the maximal pathway activation in those backgrounds by ~60% and ~45%, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: When Ste5 was the target, the apparent Hill coefficient increased from 1.5 to 1.9.
source: The apparent Hill coefficients (nH) were also moderately changed with negative feedback compared to the untargeted kinase controls—when Ste5 was the target, nH increased from 1.5 to 1.9
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: When Ste7 was negatively regulated, the apparent Hill coefficient remained 1.6.
source: while when Ste7 was negatively regulated nH remained 1.6 (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: In the incoherent feed-forward loop created by having Fus3 both activate and inhibit the transcription factor Ste12, the inhibitory connection dominates at all levels of induction resulting in a complete elimination of the downstream response.
source: In the incoherent feed-forward loop – created by having Fus3 both activate and inhibit the transcription factor Ste12 – we find that the inhibitory connection dominates at all levels of induction resulting in a complete elimination of the downstream response (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The incoherent feed-forward loop with YFP under pFUS1 promoter control created a concentration-based band-pass filter for the α-factor input.
source: In cells containing the feed-forward loop the fluorescent signal initially increased sharply as the α-factor concentration was increased from 0.1 μM to ~1 μM—however, induction with concentrations of α-factor higher than 1 μM resulted in decreasing levels of YFP fluorescence. The incoherent feed-forward loop thus created a concentration-based band-pass filter for the α-factor input.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: It is the targeted regulation of YFP by Fus3 that caused the band-pass-like behavior.
source: In a control where the phosphodegron fused to YFP was broken we observe the normal signal amplification behavior of the mating cascade (Figure 7A)—thus, it is the targeted regulation of YFP by Fus3 that caused the band-pass-like behavior.
evidence: Supported by comparison with control data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Simply co-localizing an active MAPK with a protein bearing a compatible amino acid motif that can be phosphorylated is sufficient for the functional regulation of the protein.
source: Our results suggest that while these domains may have some allosteric properties, simply co-localizing an active MAPK with a protein bearing a compatible amino acid motif that can be phosphorylated is sufficient for the functional regulation of the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results

claim: The evolution of new connections within MAPK regulation networks is only constrained by the appearance of an accessible phospho-motif and a protein-protein interaction strong enough to co-localize the new kinase-substrate pair.
source: One implication of our results is that the evolution of new connections within MAPK regulation networks is only constrained by the two criteria discussed above—namely the appearance of 1) an accessible phospho-motif; and, 2) a protein-protein interaction strong enough to co-localize the new kinase-substrate pair.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental results

claim: The proteomes of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and humans have ~3500 and >50,000 phosphorylation sites, respectively.
source: The proteomes of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and humans have ~3500 and >50,000 phosphorylation sites, respectively (Hornbeck et al., 2015, 2012; Beltrao et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hornbeck et al., 2015, 2012 and Beltrao et al., 2009

claim: Many human SNPs have been observed to create and destroy verified phospho-motifs.
source: Indeed, many human SNPs – both those associated with disease as well as apparently healthy individual variation – have been observed to create and destroy verified phospho-motifs (Hornbeck et al., 2015; Reimand and Bader, 2013; Ryu et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hornbeck et al., 2015, Reimand and Bader, 2013, and Ryu et al., 2009

claim: Fus3 is the terminal MAPK of the mating pathway of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: We utilized modular interaction domains to co-localize Fus3 – the terminal MAPK of the mating pathway of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae – with a substrate of interest.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: α-factor signals to the central MAPK kinase cascade via a surface-associated receptor.
source: α-factor signals to the central MAPK kinase cascade via a surface-associated receptor; signaling through the pathway activates Fus3, which in turn mediates signaling to a myriad of downstream effectors, directly regulating protein function and gene expression (Figure 1A) (Bardwell, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bardwell, 2004 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Upon phosphorylation, the phosphodegron interacts with a specialized F-box protein – Cdc4 – to recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase machinery (the SCF complex).
source: Upon phosphorylation, the phosphodegron interacts with a specialized F-box protein – Cdc4 – to recruit the E3 ubiquitin ligase machinery (the SCF complex), which then marks the substrate for degradation by covalently attaching a poly-ubiquitin chain (Figure 1A) (Skaar et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Skaar et al., 2013 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Cdc4 primarily acts in the nucleus.
source: Also, since Cdc4 primarily acts in the nucleus, we added a nuclear localization signal derived from SV40 large T-antigen to the N-terminus of the protein (Blondel et al., 2000; Kalderon et al., 1984)
evidence: Supported by citations to Blondel et al., 2000 and Kalderon et al., 1984

claim: In yeast constitutively expressing a single-copy fluorescent protein, fluorescence is strongly correlated with cell size.
source: In yeast constitutively expressing a single-copy fluorescent protein inserted in the genome, fluorescence (FL1-A) is strongly correlated with cell size (approximated by FSC-A)—shown by R2 values.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Normalizing fluorescence by cell size reduces the coefficient of variation of the fluorescent signal by ~67% or ~41% in untreated or treated cells, respectively.
source: Normalizing by cells size – dividing FL1-A by FSC-A – reduces the coefficient of variation (CV) of the fluorescent signal by ~67% or ~41% in untreated or treated cells, respectively (graphs on right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The fold change observed three hours post induction for the swapped interaction domains was approximately half that of the original orientation.
source: Following induction of the mating pathway with α-factor, we measured the YFP fluorescence of the cells using flow cytometry and observed qualitatively similar substrate degradation. However, the fold change observed three hours post induction for the swapped domains was approximately half that of the original orientation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Fus3 and Kss1 share many of the same targets, but also have distinct substrates, presumably as a result of the specialization of their preferences for related docking domains.
source: Fus3 and Kss1 share many of the same targets, but also have distinct substrates, presumably as a result of the specialization of their preferences for related docking domains (Reményi et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Reményi et al., 2005

claim: The response of a scaffolded signaling cascade is highly sensitive to the concentration of the scaffold protein.
source: However, the response of a scaffolded signaling cascade is highly sensitive to the concentration of the scaffold protein—with a reduction of the scaffold concentration resulting in an increase in the sensitivity of the cascade (Levchenko et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Levchenko et al., 2000

claim: A reduction of the scaffold concentration results in an increase in the sensitivity of the cascade.
source: However, the response of a scaffolded signaling cascade is highly sensitive to the concentration of the scaffold protein—with a reduction of the scaffold concentration resulting in an increase in the sensitivity of the cascade (Levchenko et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Levchenko et al., 2000

claim: All strains were built using a W303a background.
source: All strains were built using a W303a background into which each synthetic construct was integrated at either the URA, HIS, TRP or LEU genomic loci.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods
